This is no toy: the same system sped up a key matmul kernel in Gemini training by 23%, cutting overall Gemini training time by 1%. It sped up the FlashAttention kernel by up to 32.5%. It also proposed a Verilog rewrite of a highly optimized TPU arithmetic circuit, which passed correctness verification and has been integrated into the next-generation TPU. A scheduling heuristic that has run on Borg for over a year recovers an average of 0.7% of Google's global compute, saving the equivalent of building a new data center each year. zh2en:AlphaEvolve 教给你的不是「用 LLM 写代码」，而是「用: What AlphaEvolve teaches you isn't "use an LLM to write code" but "use an evaluation cascade to lock the LLM in a cage, so it only gets credit when it can actually prove itself" — that's the real secret to making code evolution work.
zh2en:AlphaEvolve 最核心的机制不是 LLM，而是 evalua: The core mechanism of AlphaEvolve isn't the LLM, it's the evaluator. After each candidate program is generated, evaluation runs in multiple stages: first the cheapest stage (e.g., unit tests, small inputs, sanity checks that finish in seconds); only candidates that pass this stage are allowed into the next one (longer benchmarks, held-out datasets, perturbed inputs); and only the final stage is the truly expensive full evaluation (e.g., a complete correctness proof, large-scale performance tests). This way, the vast majority of obviously wrong or obviously mediocre candidates are killed at the first stage, and precious evaluation compute is spent only on patches with real potential. This is the "evaluation cascade" — it compresses the most expensive step in evolutionary search from "fully evaluate every candidate" into a "pyramid funnel," and it's the key to scaling the whole pipeline to tens of thousands of samples.
zh2en:AlphaEvolve 没有押注单一模型。Gemini Flash: AlphaEvolve doesn't bet on a single model. Gemini Flash is cheap and fast and handles "breadth" — producing dozens to hundreds of ideas per round for large-scale exploration; Gemini Pro is expensive, slow, and deep, and handles "depth" — making more insightful rewrites along the promising directions Flash finds. In between, a prompt sampler picks parents from the programs database (archive) to assemble prompts, the LLM outputs candidate patches, the evaluator cascade scores them, and those that pass enter the archive to become parents for the next round — a very clean evolutionary loop. The biggest difference from FunSearch: FunSearch can only evolve a single Python function, while AlphaEvolve can evolve an entire codebase, with changes across files and modules. That's also why it can directly modify Verilog, CUDA, and the Borg scheduler.

zh2en:BM25 只看标题 · 崩得很惨 · 原因有三：\n\n1. **语:
BM25 on titles only · fails badly · for three reasons:

1. **Language mismatch**: titles are in Chinese but many queries are in English (e.g. "bluetooth speaker" doesn't match "便携蓝牙音箱" (portable Bluetooth speaker)) · BM25 finds no lexical overlap · so it falls back to a pile of junk (returning "山西红富士苹果" (Shanxi Red Fuji apples)).

2. **Intent/semantic queries** (all 0 in Tier H): e.g. "listening to music with friends at the beach" → speaker · these require semantic reasoning · pure lexical matching like BM25 can't do it.

3. **Negation and attributes** ("不要涤纶" (no polyester) · "not silk"): BM25 doesn't handle these at all.

The catalog only has 30-40 SKUs · so just **feed the entire catalog to the LLM** · and have it rank everything for each query.

zh2en:DGM 改的不是模型权重，而是 agent 的 codebase 本: DGM doesn't modify the model weights; it modifies the agent's own codebase: tool definitions, prompts, context management, and review workflows. This creates a recursive effect: the agent improves its own code editing tool, and the next-generation agent uses that better tool to modify itself, and does it better. The concrete evolution examples in the paper are telling: DGM spontaneously added patch validation, chunked handling of long contexts, and a peer-review mechanism (one agent generates a patch, another reviews it). SWE-bench went from 20.0% to 50.0%, Polyglot from 14.2% to 30.7%, significantly outperforming baselines without self-improvement or without open-ended exploration. This isn't simple scaling; it's compounding at the meta level.

zh2en:IMO 数学题这个实验特别有说服力。用 GPT-OSS-20B 搜出: The IMO math experiment is especially convincing. A retrieval harness found via search with GPT-OSS-20B was then tested on GPT-5.4-nano, GPT-5.4-mini, Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite, and Gemini-3-Flash. All five models improved, by +4.7 on average. By comparison, dense retrieval drops 0.5 points on GPT-5.4-mini and 0.9 points on Gem-3-Flash. This shows that the search didn't find black magic overfitted to one model, but a readable, transferable strategy. The authors stress this in the Discussion as well: overfitting in code space is inspectable. If-chains and hardcoded mappings are obvious at a glance, which makes it far friendlier than overfitting in weight space. On TerminalBench-2, the Haiku 4.5 version climbed to 37.6% to take first place, and the Opus 4.6 version took second with 76.4%. An open-source automatic search beat a leaderboard full of hand-tuned entries.

zh2en:LLM 作为 mutation operator 有一个已知病：面对: LLMs used as mutation operators have a known flaw: given the same prompt, they keep producing patches with very similar structure, and out of thousands of samples, perhaps fewer than one in ten carry real information. After the LLM generates a candidate, ShinkaEvolve first computes an embedding (text-embedding-3-small by default) for a similarity check. Anything too close to existing code in the archive is rejected outright and never enters the evaluation queue. Evaluation is the most expensive step (it runs real code on real benchmarks), so a novelty gate before evaluation pushes sample efficiency up another notch. This is the key change that turns evolutionary search from "brute-force sampling" into "informative sampling".

zh2en:SFR-Embedding-Mistral 在 MTEB 上 nDC: SFR-Embedding-Mistral scores nDCG@10 = 59.0 on MTEB but only 18.3 on BRIGHT. The BM25 baseline gets 14.3, and the strongest dense model without augmentation reaches only 24.3 — two-thirds lower than its MTEB score. Even more embarrassing: add GPT-4-generated chain-of-thought reasoning to the query and feed it to BM25, and BM25 overtakes every neural retriever to top the leaderboard, gaining as much as +12.2 nDCG@10. The authors' explanation: dense embedders overfit to short information-seeking queries, so on out-of-distribution, long reasoning-heavy queries they're less flexible than plain BM25. The takeaway: the "semantics" today's embedding models learn is still largely shallow, surface-level semantics.

zh2en:Schmidhuber 的 Gödel machine 要求 age: Schmidhuber's Gödel machine requires an agent to prove that a change is a "net gain" before each self-modification — theoretically elegant but impossible in practice, because most meaningful changes can't be formally proven. DGM takes a pragmatic approach: replace "proof" with "run the benchmark." Each new agent version runs on SWE-bench or Polyglot, and the score decides. This step looks simple, but it's the key to making self-improvement actually work — it turns a math problem into an engineering problem. The cost is losing theoretical guarantees; the payoff is a system that actually runs. This pragmatic shift largely set the technical direction for every self-improving agent from 2025 onward.

zh2en:The baseline BM25-on-titles approa:
The baseline BM25-on-titles approach fails badly because:

1. **Language mismatch**: Titles are in Chinese but many queries are English (e.g., "bluetooth speaker" doesn't match "便携蓝牙音箱"). BM25 finds no overlap and falls back to garbage ("山西红富士苹果").
2. **Intent/semantic queries** (tier H, all scoring 0): queries like "海边跟朋友一起听歌" (listening to music at the beach → speaker) require semantic reasoning, impossible with lexical BM25.
3. **Negation & attributes** ("不要涤纶", "not silk") aren't handled.

The catalog is small (~30-40 SKUs), so we can feed the **entire catalog to the LLM** and ask it to rank the top-5 relevant SKUs. This handles cross-lingual matching, intent reasoning, and negation in one call. BM25 remains a fallback for robustness.

zh2en:The current LLM-ranking approach s:
The current LLM-ranking approach scores 0.94 combined, with remaining weakness concentrated on the hardest intent/ambiguity queries (e.g. "reading on my kindle late at night and want to set the mood" → vintage lamp, "office gift exchange, looks high-end but not expensive" → wool scarf, "stay hydrated outdoors without carrying anything heavy" → glass bottle). These require deeper reasoning about implicit intent that a single-shot "output only sku_ids" prompt suppresses.

**Idea:** Enable brief chain-of-thought reasoning before the final answer. LLMs rank noticeably better on ambiguous/intent queries when allowed to reason first. To keep parsing robust, I instruct the model to emit a clear `FINAL:` marker and parse SKUs only from the text *after the last marker* (falling back to first-seen if no marker), so reasoning-mentioned SKUs don't pollute the ranking.

zh2en:`shinka/llm/providers/anthropic.py: `shinka/llm/providers/anthropic.py` is only 212 lines: one module-level `query_anthropic` (85) and one `query_anthropic_async` (157). The two functions are nearly identical and differ only by await. Line 108 calls `client.messages.create(...)` directly. The client is passed down from the caller and can be any of `anthropic.Anthropic`, `anthropic.AnthropicBedrock`, `anthropic.AsyncAnthropic` or `anthropic.AsyncAnthropicBedrock` (provider dispatch lives in the `_sync_constructors / _async_constructors` dicts at `shinka/llm/client.py:123-146`). The Bedrock client is built in `_constructor_configuration` at client.py:196, which only accepts AWS credentials from a few fixed environment variables. The IAM instance profile (boto3 default chain) isn't on that allowlist, so on EC2 the precheck has to be bypassed. That's why our demo needs its first monkey-patch. `NO_TEMPERATURE_MODELS` is a module-level set at `shinka/llm/kwargs.py:25`. `sample_model_kwargs` at line 128 checks whether api_model_name is in it and, if it is, omits the `temperature` field. Because it's a module-level set, you can call `.update({...})` on it right after import to add custom model ids.
zh2en:`shinka/llm/providers/pricing.csv`: `shinka/llm/providers/pricing.csv` is only 76 lines, and each row is `model_name,provider,input_price,output_price,input_price_tier2,output_price_tier2,tier_threshold,is_reasoning,think_temp_fixed,requires_reasoning`. It's loaded via `shinka/pricing/normalization.py:284 _load_llm_csv`, which reads it once with stdlib `csv.DictReader`, converts each row into a `ModelPrice` frozen dataclass (catalog.py:47), then merges it into the catalog (catalog.py:82 PricingCatalog index). It's a CSV rather than Python constants because it serves as a fallback and can also be appended to at runtime. At runtime, the catalog first tries to pull the latest prices from the models.dev API (catalog.py:23 MODELS_DEV_URL, 268 `_refresh_online`). If that fails, it falls back to this CSV (normalization.py:37 include_bundled=True). So if your model's price can't be found (e.g., Opus 4.7 isn't listed on models.dev yet), appending one row to this CSV brings cost tracking back to life without changing any Python code. The lookup APIs are `shinka/llm/providers/pricing.py:37 model_exists` and 27 `calculate_cost`, and the latter is called by `anthropic.py:28 get_anthropic_costs`. If the lookup fails, it logs a warning and falls back to 0 without blocking generations that have already completed, as the comments at anthropic.py:29-33 state explicitly.

zh2en:demo 里 `evolution/run_evo.py` 顶部三处: In the demo, three monkey-patches at the top of `evolution/run_evo.py` target exactly these points. (1) `shinka.model_availability._model_env_access_issues` lets Bedrock IAM auth through and bypasses the env var checks around client.py:196. (2) `shinka.llm.kwargs.NO_TEMPERATURE_MODELS` gets our Bedrock inference profile id added to the module-level set at kwargs.py:25 via .update. (3) `shinka.llm.providers.anthropic.query_anthropic / query_anthropic_async` rewrites the legacy `thinking={type: enabled, budget_tokens: N}` generated by kwargs.py:181-192 into Opus 4.7+'s `thinking={type: adaptive}` + `extra_body.output_config.effort` before the call. The `combined_score / public / private / text_feedback` in the dict returned by `evaluate.py` map directly to the four-line destructuring at `async_runner.py:1631`. `public` holds the visible tier E/M/H metrics, which are fed to the next generation's LLM. `private` holds the hold-out scores, which are written only to SQLite and never go into the prompt.

It found that every wrong answer pointed to the same root cause: BM25 treats the entire query as keywords, with no semantic decomposition. Nothing in the query tells you which theorem the target document is about; you first have to infer "oh, this is moral hazard" and then go find another moral hazard case. Or a programmer searches with an error message for the corresponding syntax docs, where the error text and the doc body have almost zero literal overlap. BRIGHT systematizes queries like these into 1,384 questions, covering seven StackExchange sub-sites (Biology, Economics, Psychology, Robotics, Earth Science, Stack Overflow, Sustainable Living), plus LeetCode and math Olympiad problems. The common trait: connecting the query to the gold document requires a step of domain reasoning.
zh2en:之前的 text optimizer 有个共同毛病：把历史压成一句: Earlier text optimizers share a common flaw: they compress the history into a one-line summary and stuff it into the prompt. OPRO uses 0.002 MTok/iter, GEPA 0.008, TTT-Discover 0.026, in millions of tokens. Meta-Harness uses a full 10.0 MTok/iter, a gap of three orders of magnitude. The proposer doesn't consume it all at once; it works like a real programmer: each round it greps a median of 82 files (41% historical harness source code, 40% execution traces), spanning 20+ historical candidates. This is non-Markovian: it doesn't just look at the previous version, but freely digs into early failure cases to reason. The implicit premise of this design: only in early 2026 did coding agents become just strong enough to decide for themselves what to look at.

zh2en:今天 demo 直接跑的就是这个框架。我们做了三处 monkey-p: Today's demo runs this framework directly. We applied three monkey-patches to make it work with Claude Opus 4.7 / 4.8 on Bedrock: first, we swapped its built-in OpenAI / Gemini client for a Bedrock client; second, we changed the pricing lookup from models.dev to a local table (Opus isn't on models.dev); third, we disabled the headless CLI path. The rest of the aggregate_fn contract (combined_score + public + private + text_feedback) is untouched — and that contract happens to leave room for our "three-tier evaluation": the fast, medium, and final evals are all written into aggregate_fn.
zh2en:今天 demo 里 evaluate.py 那条 `combined: In today's demo, the composite score formula in evaluate.py, `combined = 0.7·public + 0.2·heldout + 0.1·perturbed`, and the cascade gate that scores the H tier only when the E score >= 0.7 and the M score >= 0.5, are copied straight from AlphaEvolve's evaluation cascade — cheap before expensive, local before global, and nothing advances to the next tier without passing the previous one. You can think of today's demo as taking AlphaEvolve's evaluation philosophy from "a closed-source system inside Google" to an open-source setup that runs on "a single GPU + Bedrock Claude."

zh2en:传统 evolutionary code search 要么每一代只: Traditional evolutionary code search either mutates only from the best individual each generation (getting stuck in local optima) or samples uniformly (wasting budget). ShinkaEvolve organizes the population into multiple islands, each offering three parent selection strategies — weighted, power_law, and beam_search — plus migration between islands and dynamic island spawning. On the archive side, elite_selection_ratio 0.3 and crowding-based replacement maintain population diversity. The core idea: give each mutation some probability of exploring "suboptimal but high-potential" branches, so the whole search doesn't collapse around the current leader. This is the first pillar behind reaching SOTA with just 150 samples.

zh2en:入口是 `shinka/core/async_runner.py:1: The entry point is `shinka/core/async_runner.py:1002 def run(self)`. The synchronous wrapper directly calls `run_async()` (line 1017) → `_run_async()` (line 1024). The real main loop isn't a for loop but an asyncio.gather over three coroutines: `_job_monitor_task` (line 2037, monitors completion of evaluate.py subprocesses), `_proposal_coordinator_task` (line 2417, decides whether to pull another patch based on pipeline_target and max_evaluation_jobs), and `_meta_summarizer_task` (optional, runs a summary every meta_rec_interval generations). Each propose goes through `_generate_evolved_proposal` (line 2702). It first calls `sample_parent()` on the database (parents.py:89 abstract method), then `PromptSampler.sample()` (core/sampler.py:77) to build the prompt, then `LLMClient.query()` (llm/llm.py:288) to get the patch, then `apply_patch_async` (edit/async_apply.py:67) to write the patch to the file system, and finally `JobScheduler.submit_async` (launch/scheduler.py:288) to run evaluate.py via subprocess. All events go into SQLite (database/dbase.py:434 table-creation SQL).

zh2en:图 1：一块真实的双路服务器主板（Intel S2600CP4）。两: Figure 1: A real dual-socket server motherboard (Intel S2600CP4). Each of the two large heatsinks sits on a CPU, and each CPU has 4 memory slots above and 4 below; these 8 slots connect only to its own memory controller. The QPI interconnect between the two CPUs runs inside the board and isn't visible in the photo. Which CPU counts as node 0 is decided by the firmware; the labels here are only illustrative. Photo:
zh2en:图 2：两个 NUMA node。绿线是本地访问，核心经本 node: Figure 2: Two NUMA nodes. The green line is local access: a core reads its own DIMMs through its node's memory controller. The orange dashed line is remote access: it has to cross the socket interconnect to reach the other node's DIMMs.
zh2en:图 3：左边是早年的 UMA，所有 CPU 挤一条总线，通过北桥里唯: Figure 3: On the left is the early UMA design: all CPUs share one bus and read memory through the single memory controller in the northbridge, so it's equally far for everyone. On the right is today's NUMA: each CPU has its own memory controller and memory, so total bandwidth grows with the number of CPUs, at the cost of slower remote access.
zh2en:图 4：node 编号的来历。固件最清楚哪些 CPU 和内存接在一起: Figure 4: Where node numbers come from. The firmware knows best which CPUs and memory are connected together, and it records this in two ACPI tables, SRAT and SLIT. At boot, Linux reads these tables and numbers each affinity domain starting from 0.
zh2en:图 5：同样分配几页内存，四种策略的结果。local 放在当前 CP: Figure 5: The result of allocating the same few pages under four policies. local places them on the current CPU's node; bind can only use the specified node and fails when it's full; preferred tries the specified node first and spills over elsewhere when it's full; interleave places pages round-robin, half on each side.
zh2en:图 6：一次\"放错\"会同时记两笔账。进程 P 想在 node 1: Figure 6: One "misplaced" allocation is recorded twice. Process P wants to allocate on node 1, but node 1 is full, so the page lands on node 0. As a result, node 0's numa_miss goes up by 1 and node 1's numa_foreign goes up by 1.
zh2en:图 7：NUMA balancing 的工作循环。它不是一次性搬完，: Figure 7: The NUMA balancing loop. It doesn't move everything at once; it keeps sampling, tracking, and migrating.
zh2en:图 8：左边是修复前。buffer pool 大多落在 node 0: Figure 8: On the left, before the fix. Most of the buffer pool landed on node 0, and once node 0 was full, the kernel would rather swap InnoDB pages out to swap (the swap area on disk) than use the free memory on node 1. On the right, after adding interleave, each node holds 26 GB with room to spare. Data from Jeremy Cole's original post.

No subclassing needed — just pass them when constructing DatabaseConfig. Parent strategy implementations all live in `shinka/database/parents.py`: PowerLawSamplingStrategy (102), WeightedSamplingStrategy (237), BeamSearchSamplingStrategy (436), BestOfNSamplingStrategy (534), SequentialSamplingStrategy (601), all dispatched by `CombinedParentSelector` (669). Novelty rejection is in `shinka/core/novelty_judge.py:60 assess_novelty_with_rejection_sampling`: it first checks embedding cosine similarity (line 89, `database.compute_similarity`) and rejects if it exceeds `code_embed_sim_threshold` (config.py:59, default 0.99); if a novelty LLM is also configured, it runs an additional LLM judgment (line 122), retrying up to `max_novelty_attempts` times (config.py:58, default 3). All reject decisions happen before evaluate, so no evaluation budget is wasted.

These queries require deeper reasoning about **implicit intent**, but the current one-shot prompt that "only outputs sku_ids" suppresses that reasoning.

**Idea**: Let the LLM do a short chain-of-thought before its final answer. On ambiguity/intent queries, LLMs that reason first and then answer rank noticeably better. zh2en:本次 demo 用的 ShinkaEvolve（arXiv:2509: The ShinkaEvolve used in this demo (arXiv:2509.19349, 2025-09) is the productized follow-up Robert Lange built at Sakana AI. A co-author of DGM became the first author of ShinkaEvolve. The technical lineage is clear: DGM proved that the "archive + LLM mutation + benchmark validation" approach works, but its sample efficiency is poor (it needs thousands of samples). ShinkaEvolve adds parent sampling, novelty rejection, and a bandit-based LLM ensemble to the same framework, cutting the sample count to 150 while still reaching SOTA. DGM is the prototype; ShinkaEvolve is the usable tool. Today's harness self-evolution demo essentially runs the paradigm DGM established.

zh2en:标注流程精心设计：先从 StackExchange 选带 accep: The annotation pipeline is carefully designed: first, high-quality StackExchange posts with an accepted answer or >5 votes and a URL in the answer are selected, and the web pages those URLs point to are split into passages as gold positives. The key is the hard negatives: **annotators search Google for the post title or LLM-extracted keywords and pick pages from the results that are "topically very similar but can't actually answer the question"**. Each question gets up to 5 Google-mined hard negatives, split into several negative passages. Everything is first annotated by a CS student, then independently verified by two domain PhDs, and an item is kept only if both experts agree. This "Google-mined hard negatives" idea is well worth borrowing: no matter how capable machines get, it's hard to automatically generate distractors that are "right on topic but don't solve the problem". Only humans with a search engine can produce them.

zh2en:框架默认同时接入 gpt-5-mini、gemini-3-flash: By default, the framework connects to multiple models at once, including gpt-5-mini, gemini-3-flash, gemini-3.1-pro, and gpt-5.4. Each mutation isn't tied to one fixed model. Instead, a multi-armed bandit dynamically adjusts weights based on history: "whose patches are more likely to be selected into the archive." Cheap small models cast a wide net for exploration, while expensive flagship models are only called when the bandit thinks it's worth it. Combined with max_api_costs as a hard USD budget cap, the whole run spends money where it counts. This is also why it can claim to be cost-efficient and to democratize open-ended discovery.

zh2en:站在 2026 年回看，DGM 是 self-improving a: Looking back from 2026, DGM is the starting point of the self-improving agent lineage. It was the first to bring Schmidhuber's 2003 Gödel machine out of theory and into something you can actually run, replacing the impossible requirement of "proving every change is a net gain" with "run SWE-bench and check the score." More importantly, it brought the archive idea from open-endedness research into agent self-improvement: instead of greedily pushing the best solution forward, it keeps an entire evolutionary tree, failed branches included. Today, Sakana's ShinkaEvolve and the various self-evolving harnesses all trace their lineage back to it.

The paper ran a very clean ablation: scores-only (34.6 median / 41.3 best), scores+summary (34.9 / 38.7), and full Meta-Harness (50.0 / 56.7). The best score of the summary version was even 2.6 points lower than scores-only. The authors' interpretation is blunt: LLM-generated summaries crush the diagnostic information. A harness bug may only blow up dozens of steps later, and you need to see the full trajectory to trace it back to the original faulty retrieval logic. It's like debugging a distributed system: error codes alone are useless, and you have to read the full log. This insight also explains why earlier approaches like GEPA and TextGrad hit a ceiling.

zh2en:跟 AlphaEvolve、AFlow 那种精心设计的进化框架不一样: Unlike carefully engineered evolutionary frameworks such as AlphaEvolve and AFlow, Meta-Harness's outer loop is extremely minimal: no parent selection rule, no archive structure, just a Pareto frontier. In the authors' words, it's deliberately minimal—all decisions about diagnosis and modification are handed to the coding agent. The entire history lives in the file system, and the agent looks up whatever it wants. The philosophy is very Bitter Lesson: once the search space is accessible, a general-purpose agent beats hand-designed heuristics. On text classification, Meta-Harness matches in 4 rounds what OpenEvolve and TTT-Discover reach in 60, a 10× speedup. The algorithm isn't clever; it just doesn't overcomplicate things.

zh2en:这是 DGM 最反直觉、也最重要的设计。传统优化会丢掉分数低的分支，: This is DGM's most counterintuitive and most important design choice. Traditional optimization discards low-scoring branches and keeps only the best. DGM does the opposite: it maintains an archive that keeps every agent from every generation, including those that look like failures at the time. The next generation isn't picked from the best. Instead, a parent is sampled "interestingly" from the archive, and the foundation model generates a new variant from it. This forms a constantly branching tree that explores many paths in parallel. Why do it this way? In open-ended search, today's failure is often the stepping stone to tomorrow's breakthrough. An intermediate form may not be useful on its own, but one more step on top of it can open a new dimension. The idea comes directly from Jeff Clune's group and its years of open-endedness research (the Quality-Diversity and MAP-Elites line of work).
zh2en:这是「用 LLM 做真·算法发现」这个 field 的开山之作 ——: This is the founding work of the field of "real algorithm discovery with LLMs". Before it, FunSearch could only evolve a single function. AlphaEvolve was the first to scale evolutionary code search to an entire codebase, and it went straight into high-stakes production systems like Google Borg, Gemini training kernels, and TPU Verilog. It's closed-source, with Early Access available only to a small number of academic users. The Shinka and DGM you can pip install from GitHub today are essentially open-source descendants of this paper's ideas. Understanding AlphaEvolve = understanding the original design behind every code evolution framework today.
zh2en:这是今天 harness self-evolution demo 背: This is the engine running directly behind today's harness self-evolution demo, and currently the only code-evolution framework you can actually pip install and use. Closed-source heavyweight tools like AlphaEvolve often need thousands of samples to converge. ShinkaEvolve reaches SOTA on circle packing in just 150 samples. Its author, Robert Lange, is also the first author of the Darwin Gödel Machine (DGM), so ShinkaEvolve is essentially the productized version of DGM: the same team turned a research prototype into an engineering framework. It comes from Sakana AI, the Tokyo lab founded by Transformer paper author Llion Jones.

zh2en:顶层 shinka/ 只有 8 个真正在跑的子模块。`shinka/: Top-level shinka/ has only 8 submodules that actually run. `shinka/core/` is the main evolution loop (async_runner.py at 6254 lines + EvolutionConfig in config.py + run_shinka_eval in wrap_eval.py + novelty_judge.py + sampler.py). `shinka/database/` is SQLite-backed archive/island storage (DatabaseConfig + Program dataclass in dbase.py + 5 ParentSamplingStrategy types in parents.py). `shinka/llm/` is the provider-agnostic dispatch layer (LLMClient / AsyncLLMClient in llm.py + sample_model_kwargs in kwargs.py + the bandit in prioritization.py). `shinka/llm/providers/` has one file per cloud vendor (anthropic.py / openai.py / gemini.py / deepseek.py / local_openai.py / headless.py) plus a pricing.csv. `shinka/edit/` handles applying LLM-generated patches (apply_diff.py does search-and-replace, apply_full.py overwrites the whole file, marker_validation.py checks EVOLVE-BLOCK-START/END markers). `shinka/launch/` is just a subprocess wrapper (LocalJobConfig / SlurmJobConfig / JobScheduler) that runs evaluate.py as a child process. `shinka/pricing/` is the runtime pricing catalog, loaded by merging the CSV + models.dev API.
